newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Gore to keep Syrian arms discussions confidential.
newsitem.headline: Gore to keep Syrian arms discussions confidential.

text.p: U.S. Vice President Al Gore on Sunday refused to speak in public about a proposed South African arms sale with Syria, saying South Africa was already fully aware of Washington's opposition to the deal.

In an interview with Reuters on Saturday, Gore said: "I treat opportunities to discuss such sensitive issues with President Nelson Mandela and Deputy President Thabo Mbeki the same way I treat such conversations with President Clinton -- as matters that must be dealt with confidentially."
Gore was expected to raise the matter with Mbeki in private talks on Monday.

Gore is in South Africa at the head of a high-level U.S. delegation that includes five cabinet secretaries for three days of talks to deepen the cooperation between the two countries on trade, economics, science, education, health and the environment. Mbeki heads the South African team to the binational commission.

At a round table with a dozen South African journalists, Gore was asked repeatedly about the Syrian arms deal but refused to be drawn in and instead played down its effect on U.S.-South African relations, which he described as excellent.
"Friends will sometimes have disagreements. Friends work through their disagreements in a mutually respectful way," he said.
"That is a decision that South Africa makes so it's not for me to speak on a decision that is South Africa's. You know my feelings," he said.
The issue also came up after Gore paid a courtesy call on Mandela, who was asked about the controversy. He said Mbeki was dealing with the issue.

Gore also toured the prison on Robben Island, where Mandela was held for 18 years. Earlier, he visited the Crossroads black township, seeing at first hand the grinding poverty in which millions of black South Africans live.

The United States and South Africa exchanged angry words last month when the United States warned South Africa against going through with a proposed $650 million sale of a laser-guided tank firing control system to Syria, which Washington classifies as a "state sponsor of terrorism".

Mandela angrily rejected the U.S. criticism as an affront to his country's national pride and independence. Meanwhile Washington warned that providing the system to Syria would result in South Africa losing $120 million of U.S. aid.
But both countries now seem anxious to defuse the issue and Gore welcomed South Africa's stated intention to consider the issue carefully before taking a decision.

Gore said he believed the United States had as strong an interest in seeing South Africa's transition to multi-racial democracy succeed as it had in Russia's building of a free market democratic society.

"In a world beset with racial and ethnic conflicts, from Bosnia to Nagorno-Karabakh to Rwanda, Burundi, Zaire to Cambodia to Cyprus, if South Africa can make this transition, it will be a permanent beacon of hope to humankind," he said.

Gore said the United States had created binational commissions to pursue cooperation across a broad range of issues with only two countries -- South Africa and Russia. The Vice President heads the U.S. side to both and has emerged as a leading voice in U.S. foreign policy.

He is also increasingly seen as Clinton's designated heir apparent. Many guests to a reception held in Gore's honour at the U.S. ambassador's residence Saturday said they had come the see and hear the man who could become the next President of the United States.
